## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dhātu Sutta* (Iti 51; It 3.2, PTS It 45), also titled the *Dhātusutta* and translated as "Elements", is a short discourse from the *Tikanipāta* section of the *Itivuttaka* [SuttaCentral]. The sutta expounds three basic properties or elements (*dhātu*): the element of form (*rūpadhātu*), the formless element (*arūpadhātu*), and the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*) [SuttaCentral]. In the accompanying verse portion, those who fully comprehend the form element, do not cling to the formless realms, and find release in cessation are said to leave death behind; having personally experienced the deathless realm and realized the "relinquishing of all acquisitions" (*upadhipaṭinissagga*), the uncorrupted (*anāsavo*) Buddha teaches this sorrowless, unsoiled state [SuttaCentral; de La Vallée Poussin 1923]. Louis de La Vallée Poussin cited this specific verse occurrence of *upadhipaṭinissagga* in his commentary on the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* as a direct canonical Pali counterpart to the Sanskrit Nirvāṇa formula *sarvopadhipratiniḥsarga* [de La Vallée Poussin 1923].

SuttaCentral records a direct parallel in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama*, SĀ 462 (三界) [SuttaCentral]. This relationship is supported by DharmaNexus, which computes an alignment between Iti 51 (§0.3–1.1) and SĀ 462 (T 99, fascicle 17, at T02n0099_p0118a11–18, plausibility score 75) [DharmaNexus]. In Pali-internal text reuse, DharmaNexus identifies 54 matching segments across 13 texts [DharmaNexus]. These include shared verse segments with the *Santatara Sutta* (Iti 73, segments §3.1–5.1 ↔ §4.1–6.1 at a 0.98 similarity level) and prose parallels with the *Magga Saṁyutta* (SN 45, §2.1–2.4), the *Tikanipāta* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 3), and various other *Itivuttaka* discourses (such as Iti 52, 53, 55, 72, and 95) [DharmaNexus]. Modern translations include English renderings by Bhikkhu Sujato alongside 18 other translations across 16 languages cataloged on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral].
